# Overview
Relevant source files The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page: - [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) - [README.md](README.md) - [config/appsettings.json](config/appsettings.json)
This document provides a high-level introduction to the IoTPowerShellAgent system, its purpose, core capabilities, and architectural components. For detailed information about specific subsystems, see [Architecture](#2) for component deep-dives, [Operational Modes](#3) for execution modes, and [Deployment and Installation](#7) for production setup. --- ## Purpose and Scope IoTPowerShellAgent is a Windows Service application that enables remote execution of PowerShell scripts on Windows devices through Azure IoT Hub. The system receives script execution requests via IoT Hub Direct Methods, executes them in isolated PowerShell runspaces with concurrency controls, and returns structured results including output, errors, and telemetry. This enables centralized management and automation of distributed Windows IoT devices. The agent runs as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` to ensure PowerShell scripts have full system privileges for device management tasks. All communication with Azure IoT Hub uses device-authenticated connections with support for multiple transport protocols (AMQP, MQTT, HTTPS). **Sources:** [README.md:1-13](), [CONTRIBUTING.md:23-30]() --- ## Core Capabilities ### Remote PowerShell Execution The agent listens for `ExecuteScript` Direct Methods from Azure IoT Hub and executes PowerShell scripts using the `PowerShellExecutor` class. Scripts can be provided as inline PowerShell or base64-encoded content. The system supports: - **Concurrent execution control** via `SemaphoreSlim` (configurable via `MaxConcurrentRunspaces`) - **Timeout enforcement** using cancellation tokens (configurable via `ScriptTimeoutSeconds`) - **Output stream capture** for all six PowerShell streams (Output, Error, Debug, Verbose, Warning, Information) - **Automatic compression** of large responses (>1KB) using GZip ### Azure IoT Hub Integration The `IoTHubService` class manages all cloud connectivity: - **Direct Method handlers** for script execution requests - **Telemetry streaming** for log messages and operational events - **Device Twin updates** with system metrics (CPU, memory, AD/Entra domain information) - **Transport protocol support** for AMQP, MQTT, and HTTPS ### Multiple Operational Modes The application entry point in `Program.Main` dispatches to five distinct modes based on command-line arguments: | Mode | Trigger | Use Case | |------|---------|----------| | **Windows Service** | `UserInteractive=false` | Production deployment with lifecycle management | | **Console** | `dotnet run` | Development with IoT Hub connectivity | | **Debug** | `--debug` / `-d` | Interactive REPL without IoT Hub | | **Test** | `--test` / `-t` | One-time script execution for validation | | **Service Installer** | `install`/`uninstall`/`start`/`stop` | Service configuration and management | For operational mode details, see [Operational Modes](#3). **Sources:** [README.md:6-13](), [README.md:67-130](), [config/appsettings.json:1-9]() --- ## System Architecture The following diagram maps the high-level system components to their primary code entities: ```mermaid graph TB subgraph "Entry Point" ProgramMain["Program.Main

(LocalIoTTester.cs)"] end ProgramMain -->|"Service Mode"| PSExecService ProgramMain -->|"Install/Uninstall"| ServiceInstaller ProgramMain -->|"Debug/Test Mode"| LocalTester ProgramMain -->|"Console Mode"| IoTHubSvc PSExecService --> IoTHubSvc IoTHubSvc --> PSExecutor IoTHubSvc --> ScriptExecResponse PSExecutor --> PSExecResult PSExecutor --> PSErrorDetails IoTHubSvc --> SettingsSvc IoTHubSvc --> PriorityMgr PSExecutor --> SettingsSvc PSExecutor --> JsonObject PSExecService --> EnvMetrics PSExecService --> ProcessUtil EnvMetrics --> PSExecutor ProcessUtil --> WinApiInterop LocalTester --> PSExecutor ``` **Core Component Responsibilities:** - **Program.Main**: Application entry point that dispatches to appropriate operational mode - **PowerShellExecutorService**: Windows Service host with lifecycle management, auto-updates, and status reporting - **IoTHubService**: Central orchestrator for Azure IoT Hub communication and Direct Method handling - **PowerShellExecutor**: Script execution engine with runspace management and concurrency throttling - **SettingsService**: Singleton configuration provider loading from `appsettings.json` - **EnvironmentMetricsCollector**: System identity collector (AD domain, Entra status, network information) - **PowerShellExecutionResult**: Structured result object containing script output, errors, and execution metadata - **LocalIoTTester**: Offline testing harness for development without IoT Hub connectivity **Sources:** [README.md:15-28](), Diagram 1 from context --- ## Script Execution Flow The following sequence diagram shows how a script execution request flows through the system, mapping to specific classes and methods: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant IoTHub as "Azure IoT Hub" participant IoTHS as "IoTHubService" participant PPM as "ProcessPriorityManager" participant Sem as "SemaphoreSlim
(MaxConcurrentRunspaces)" participant PSE as "PowerShellExecutor" participant PS as "PowerShell Runspace" participant JSON as "JsonObject" IoTHub->>IoTHS: "ExecuteScript Direct Method" Note over IoTHS: "ExecuteScriptMethodHandler()" IoTHS->>IoTHS: "Validate payload size ≤ 10MB" IoTHS->>IoTHS: "Decode base64 if IsBase64Encoded=true" IoTHS->>PPM: "ElevateProcessPriority()" IoTHS->>Sem: "WaitAsync(cancellationToken)" Sem-->>IoTHS: "Slot acquired" IoTHS->>PSE: "ExecutePowerShellAsync(script, token)" Note over PSE: "Creates isolated runspace
InitialSessionState.CreateDefault2()" PSE->>PS: "AddScript(script).InvokeAsync()" PS-->>PSE: "PSObject results / ErrorRecord" alt "Complex objects" PSE->>JSON: "ConvertToJson(psObjects)" JSON-->>PSE: "JSON string" end PSE-->>IoTHS: "PowerShellExecutionResult" IoTHS->>Sem: "Release()" IoTHS->>PPM: "RestoreProcessPriority()" alt "Response > 1KB" IoTHS->>IoTHS: "GZip compress + base64 encode" end IoTHS->>IoTHub: "ScriptExecutionResponse
(status 200/400/408/500)" ``` **Key Execution Steps:** 1. **Request validation**: [IoTHubService.cs]() validates payload size (≤10MB) and decodes base64-encoded scripts 2. **Priority elevation**: `ProcessPriorityManager.ElevateProcessPriority()` temporarily sets process priority to HIGH 3. **Concurrency control**: `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync()` enforces maximum concurrent runspaces (default: 2) 4. **Script execution**: `PowerShellExecutor.ExecutePowerShellAsync()` creates an isolated runspace and executes the script 5. **Object serialization**: Complex PowerShell objects are serialized to JSON via `JsonObject.ConvertToJson()` 6. **Response compression**: Large responses are GZip-compressed and base64-encoded 7. **Priority restoration**: Process priority returns to NORMAL after execution completes For detailed information on the execution pipeline, see [PowerShell Execution Engine](#2.2). **Sources:** [README.md:133-155](), Diagram 3 from context --- ## Configuration The system uses a centralized configuration model managed by the `SettingsService` singleton. Configuration is loaded from `appsettings.json` with automatic file creation if missing: | Setting | Description | Default | |---------|-------------|---------| | `IoTHubConnectionString` | Azure IoT Hub device connection string | (required) | | `DeviceId` | IoT Hub device identifier | (required) | | `ModuleId` | IoT Edge module identifier (optional) | `""` | | `ScriptTimeoutSeconds` | Maximum script execution time before cancellation | `300` | | `MaxConcurrentRunspaces` | Maximum concurrent PowerShell executions | `2` | | `IsActivityNode` | Enable activity node mode for workflow integration | `false` | | `ActivityLogThreshold` | Log size threshold for activity nodes (characters) | `1000` | | `TransportType` | IoT Hub transport protocol (Amqp/Mqtt/Http1) | `Amqp` | The `SettingsService` loads configuration from multiple paths with fallback logic: 1. Current directory (`./appsettings.json`) 2. Executable directory (`Path.GetDirectoryName(Assembly.Location)`) 3. Creates default template if not found For complete configuration details, see [Configuration Management](#2.4). **Sources:** [config/appsettings.json:1-9](), [README.md:37-51]() --- ## Security Model The agent implements a high-privilege security model for device management: - **Service Account**: Runs as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` to provide unrestricted access for management scripts - **Authentication**: Uses Azure IoT Hub device-level authentication with connection strings - **Access Control**: Script execution access is controlled entirely through IoT Hub permissions - **Audit Trail**: All script executions are logged to Windows Event Log and IoT Hub telemetry ⚠️ **Security Consideration**: Because scripts execute with SYSTEM privileges, IoT Hub access must be tightly controlled. Only trusted devices should be granted `ExecuteScript` Direct Method permissions. Review [Security Considerations](#7.2) for production deployment best practices. **Sources:** [README.md:173-181](), [README.md:118-131]() --- ## Getting Started To begin using IoTPowerShellAgent: 1. **Development Setup**: See [Getting Started with Development](#6.1) for prerequisites and build instructions 2. **Local Testing**: Use debug mode (`dotnet run -- --debug`) for offline testing, documented in [Debug and Test Modes](#3.1) 3. **Deployment**: Follow the [Installation and Configuration](#7.1) guide for production Windows Service deployment 4. **Azure IoT Hub Setup**: Configure IoT Hub connection string in `appsettings.json` and test connectivity For troubleshooting common issues, see [Troubleshooting and FAQ](#8). **Sources:** [README.md:23-36](), [README.md:67-116](), [CONTRIBUTING.md:23-43]()

# Architecture
Relevant source files The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page: - [README.md](README.md) - [config/appsettings.json](config/appsettings.json) - [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs](src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs) - [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs](src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs)
## Purpose and Scope This document provides a comprehensive overview of the IoTPowerShellAgent system architecture, including the major components, their interactions, and the architectural patterns employed. It describes the layered structure, core execution flows, and how the system achieves its goal of executing PowerShell scripts remotely via Azure IoT Hub. For detailed information on specific subsystems, see: - IoT Hub communication patterns and device twin management: [IoT Hub Integration](#2.1) - PowerShell script execution details and runspace management: [PowerShell Execution Engine](#2.2) - Windows Service lifecycle and operational modes: [Windows Service Hosting](#2.3) - Configuration loading and environment metrics: [Configuration Management](#2.4) - Error handling strategies and logging infrastructure: [Error Handling and Logging](#2.5) ## System Overview IoTPowerShellAgent is structured as a multi-layered Windows application that bridges Azure IoT Hub cloud services with local PowerShell script execution. The system can operate in five distinct modes (Windows Service, Console, Debug, Test, and Service Installer), all dispatched through a single entry point in [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Program.cs](). The architecture prioritizes asynchronous execution, resource throttling, and comprehensive telemetry to support reliable operation on potentially resource-constrained IoT devices. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:1-614](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:1-684](), [README.md:1-197]() ## Architectural Layers The system is organized into three primary layers, each with distinct responsibilities: ### Layer 1: Service Layer The Service Layer manages application lifecycle and operational mode dispatch. The `Program.Main` method analyzes command-line arguments and environment state to determine which operational mode to enter. In production deployments, the `PowerShellExecutorService` class provides Windows Service hosting with lifecycle management (Start, Stop, Pause, Continue). **Key Components:** - `Program.Main` - Entry point and mode dispatcher - `PowerShellExecutorService` - Windows Service host implementing `ServiceBase` - Service installer logic for Windows Service registration **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Services/](https://github.com/Calvindd2f/IoTPowerShellAgent/tree/main/src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Services) ### Layer 2: Core Execution Layer The Core Execution Layer handles the primary business logic: communicating with Azure IoT Hub and executing PowerShell scripts. This layer implements the request-response cycle for the `ExecuteScript` direct method. **Key Components:** - `IoTHubService` - Manages `DeviceClient` or `ModuleClient` connections, handles direct methods, sends telemetry, updates device twins - `PowerShellExecutor` - Creates isolated PowerShell runspaces, executes scripts with timeout support, captures all output streams **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:1-614](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:1-684]() ### Layer 3: Support Components Support Components provide cross-cutting concerns including configuration, performance monitoring, serialization, and error handling. **Key Components:** - `SettingsService` - Singleton configuration manager loading from `appsettings.json` - `EnvironmentMetricsCollector` - Gathers AD domain, Entra Connect, and network information - `ProcessUtil` - Retrieves CPU and memory metrics via P/Invoke - `WindowsApiInterop` - P/Invoke declarations for kernel32.dll, psapi.dll, advapi32.dll - `JsonObject` - PowerShell object to JSON serialization - `PowerShellErrorDetails` - Structured error reporting with inner exception chains **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/](https://github.com/Calvindd2f/IoTPowerShellAgent/tree/main/src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Utilities/](https://github.com/Calvindd2f/IoTPowerShellAgent/tree/main/src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Utilities) ## Core Component Relationships ```mermaid graph TB subgraph ServiceLayer["Service Layer"] ProgramMain["Program.Main

The Service Layer initializes the Core Layer, which depends on Support Components for configuration and utilities. All telemetry flows through `IoTHubService.SendTelemetryAsync()` to the Azure IoT Hub telemetry stream. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:17-574](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:17-675](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Services/](https://github.com/Calvindd2f/IoTPowerShellAgent/tree/main/src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Services) ## Script Execution Data Flow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant AzureIoT as "Azure IoT Hub" participant IoTHubSvc as "IoTHubService

Key control points include validation at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:164-202](), semaphore-based throttling at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:264](), and automatic GZip compression for large payloads at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:296-309](). **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:207-365](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:254-603]() ## Key Architectural Patterns ### Concurrency Control with SemaphoreSlim The system implements semaphore-based throttling to prevent resource exhaustion on IoT devices with limited CPU and memory. The `_executionSemaphore` static field in `PowerShellExecutor` limits concurrent runspace creation to `MaxConcurrentRunspaces` (default: 2, configurable in [config/appsettings.json:8]()). This is critical because PowerShell runspaces consume significant memory (50-100MB each). ``` Key Implementation Points: - Semaphore initialization: PowerShellExecutor.cs:49-63 - Semaphore acquisition: PowerShellExecutor.cs:264 - Semaphore release: PowerShellExecutor.cs:275 (in finally block) - Configuration: appsettings.json MaxConcurrentRunspaces ``` **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:32-63](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:254-277](), [config/appsettings.json:8]() ### Async/Await with Cancellation Tokens All potentially long-running operations use `async`/`await` patterns with `CancellationToken` support to prevent blocking the IoT Hub listener thread. The `IoTHubService.ExecuteScriptMethodHandler` creates a `CancellationTokenSource` with a timeout derived from `ScriptTimeoutSeconds` configuration (default: 300 seconds). This token propagates through `PowerShellExecutor.ExecutePowerShellAsync` to `Task.Run` wrapping the synchronous `PowerShell.Invoke()` call. ``` Timeout Chain: 1. IoTHubService.cs:215 - Create CancellationTokenSource with timeout 2. IoTHubService.cs:281 - Pass token to ExecutePowerShellAsync 3. PowerShellExecutor.cs:264 - Pass to SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync 4. PowerShellExecutor.cs:270 - Pass to Task.Run for background execution 5. PowerShellExecutor.cs:308,400,413 - ThrowIfCancellationRequested checks ``` **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:215](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:281](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:254-277]() ### Singleton Configuration Pattern The `SettingsService` class implements the thread-safe singleton pattern for centralized configuration management. All components access configuration through `SettingsService.Instance` rather than passing configuration objects through constructors. This simplifies dependency management but creates an implicit global dependency. ``` Singleton Implementation: - Static Instance property: SettingsService class - Thread-safe initialization: Double-check locking pattern - Lazy loading: Configuration loaded on first access - File fallback: Searches multiple paths if appsettings.json not found ``` **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/](https://github.com/Calvindd2f/IoTPowerShellAgent/tree/main/src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core) ### Event-Driven Output Capture PowerShell provides six output streams (Output, Error, Debug, Verbose, Warning, Information), each exposed as a `PSDataCollection` with `DataAdded` events. The `PowerShellExecutor.BindEvents()` method attaches event handlers for all six streams at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:210-249](). Each handler processes new items incrementally by tracking a counter (`_debugLinesProcessed`, `_errorLinesProcessed`, etc.) to avoid reprocessing items. ``` Event Handler Pattern: 1. BindEvents() attaches handlers before script execution 2. DataAdded event fires when PowerShell writes to stream 3. Handler iterates from last processed index to collection.Count 4. Each message sent via ILogCallback.OnLog() 5. Counters prevent duplicate processing ``` **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:79-249]() ### Interface-Based Logging Abstraction The `ILogCallback` interface at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:680-683]() provides abstraction for logging output. Multiple implementations serve different purposes: | Implementation | Purpose | Target | |---|---|---| | `EventLogCallback` | Production logging | Windows Event Log + IoT Hub telemetry | | `CapturingLogCallback` | Test validation | In-memory buffer for assertions | | `TestLogCallback` | Development debugging | Console output | | `IoTHubService` (self) | Default fallback | IoT Hub telemetry stream | The `IoTHubService` implements `ILogCallback` and forwards logs to Azure IoT Hub as telemetry at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:521-563](). The `SendTelemetryAsync` call uses fire-and-forget pattern (`Task.Run` without await) to prevent log telemetry from blocking execution. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:680-683](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:521-563]() ## Configuration and Settings Architecture ```mermaid graph LR subgraph Sources["Configuration Sources"] AppSettingsFile["appsettings.json

Runtime metrics collected by `EnvironmentMetricsCollector` and `ProcessUtil` aggregate into device twin reported properties. The `PowerShellExecutorService` periodically calls `UpdateTwinAsync()` with comprehensive status information. **Configuration File Structure:** ```json { "IoTHubConnectionString": "Connection string or empty for credential-based auth", "DeviceId": "Device identifier", "ModuleId": "Module identifier (empty for device, set for IoT Edge module)", "IsActivityNode": "Boolean flag for workflow integration", "ActivityLogThreshold": "Maximum log messages before throttling (default: 1000)", "ScriptTimeoutSeconds": "Script execution timeout (default: 300)", "MaxConcurrentRunspaces": "Semaphore limit for concurrent executions (default: 2)", "TransportType": "mqtt|amqp|http1|mqtt_websocket_only|amqp_websocket_only" } ``` **Sources:** [config/appsettings.json:1-10](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:28-32](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:35-44]() ## Deployment and Operational Models The system supports five distinct operational modes, all dispatched through `Program.Main`: | Mode | Trigger | Use Case | IoT Hub Connection | |---|---|---|---| | **Windows Service** | `Environment.UserInteractive == false` | Production deployment with auto-start | Yes | | **Console** | `dotnet run` (no args) | Development and testing | Yes | | **Debug** | `--debug` or `-d` | Interactive REPL for local testing | No | | **Test** | `--test` or `-t` | One-time script execution | No | | **Service Installer** | `install`/`uninstall`/`start`/`stop` | Service lifecycle management | N/A | ### Windows Service Mode In production, the application runs as a Windows Service configured to start automatically. The `PowerShellExecutorService` class extends `ServiceBase` and implements lifecycle methods (`OnStart`, `OnStop`, `OnPause`, `OnContinue`). The service is configured to run as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` through the installer, giving executed PowerShell scripts full system privileges. ``` Service Lifecycle: 1. Service Control Manager starts service process 2. Program.Main detects Environment.UserInteractive == false 3. Program.Main calls ServiceBase.Run(new PowerShellExecutorService()) 4. OnStart() initializes IoTHubService and connects 5. Service listens for direct methods until OnStop() 6. OnStop() disposes IoTHubService and cleans up resources ``` **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Services/](https://github.com/Calvindd2f/IoTPowerShellAgent/tree/main/src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Services), [README.md:117-131]() ### Debug and Test Modes Debug and Test modes use `LocalIoTTester` to execute PowerShell scripts without IoT Hub connectivity. This enables offline development and automated testing. Debug mode provides an interactive REPL accepting commands like `Get-Date`, `metrics`, `sample`, and `base64:`. Test mode executes a single script and exits. ``` LocalIoTTester Features: - ExecuteScriptLocally() - Direct PowerShellExecutor invocation - TestWithSampleScript() - Predefined test scenarios - TestEnvironmentMetrics() - Validate metrics collection - No DeviceClient/ModuleClient instantiation - Console output for immediate feedback ``` **Sources:** [README.md:69-107]() ## Resource Management and Performance ### Process Priority Elevation The `ProcessPriorityManager` class temporarily elevates process priority to `ProcessPriorityClass.High` during script execution at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:211-212](). This ensures PowerShell scripts receive CPU time even on busy systems. Priority automatically restores to `Normal` via `Dispose()` pattern in a `using` statement, guaranteeing cleanup even if exceptions occur. ### Memory and CPU Monitoring The `ProcessUtil` class uses P/Invoke to query accurate memory and CPU usage via `kernel32.dll` and `psapi.dll`. This bypasses managed `Process` class APIs which can be inaccurate or slow. The `GetProcessMemoryInfo()` P/Invoke returns working set size, private bytes, and page file usage. CPU percentage calculation uses `GetProcessTimes()` to compute delta between measurements. ``` P/Invoke Performance Metrics: - WorkingSet: Physical memory (RAM) currently in use - PrivateMemorySize: Memory allocated exclusively to process - PageFileUsage: Virtual memory committed on disk - CPU Usage %: (UserTime + KernelTime) / WallClockTime * 100 ``` **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Utilities/](https://github.com/Calvindd2f/IoTPowerShellAgent/tree/main/src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Utilities) ### GZip Compression for Large Payloads IoT Hub direct method responses have size limitations. The `IoTHubService.ExecuteScriptMethodHandler` automatically GZip compresses response output if it exceeds 1KB at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:296-309](). Compressed data is base64-encoded. The response includes `IsCompressed`, `OriginalSize`, and `CompressedSize` fields to enable client-side decompression. This typically achieves 60-80% size reduction for JSON output. ``` Compression Flow: 1. Check if Output.Length > 1024 bytes 2. UTF8 encode output string to byte[] 3. CompressGZip(bytes) using GZipStream 4. Compare compressed size to original 5. If smaller, Base64 encode and set IsCompressed=true 6. Include OriginalSize and CompressedSize in response ``` **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:296-309](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:370-380]() ## Error Handling Architecture ### Structured Error Reporting The `PowerShellErrorDetails` class provides structured error information including recursive inner exception chains. When PowerShell execution fails, `PowerShellExecutor` creates `PowerShellErrorDetails` instances from `ErrorRecord` objects at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:434]() using `FromErrorRecord()` static method. These details populate the `ScriptExecutionResponse.ErrorDetails` list, enabling rich client-side error analysis. ``` PowerShellErrorDetails Structure: - Message: Primary error message - ExceptionType: Fully qualified exception type name - StackTrace: PowerShell script stack trace - InnerException: Recursive PowerShellErrorDetails for inner exceptions - CategoryInfo: ErrorCategory enumeration value - FullyQualifiedErrorId: Unique error identifier - TargetObject: Object that caused the error (if available) - ScriptStackTrace: PowerShell-specific stack trace with line numbers ``` **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:426-465](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:594-597]() ### HTTP Status Code Mapping The `ExecuteScriptMethodHandler` maps execution outcomes to appropriate HTTP status codes: - **200 OK**: Successful execution (even if PowerShell script had errors) - **400 Bad Request**: Invalid request payload (null, malformed JSON, validation failure) - **408 Request Timeout**: Script exceeded `ScriptTimeoutSeconds` or was cancelled - **500 Internal Server Error**: Unexpected exception in handler or executor This mapping enables clients to distinguish between client errors (400), timeout issues (408), and system failures (500) without parsing error messages. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:229-361]() ## Summary The IoTPowerShellAgent architecture prioritizes reliability, observability, and resource efficiency for IoT deployments. Key architectural decisions include: 1. **Layered separation of concerns**: Service hosting, core execution, and utilities isolated for testability 2. **Semaphore-based concurrency control**: Prevents memory exhaustion on resource-constrained devices 3. **Async/await with cancellation**: Non-blocking execution with timeout enforcement 4. **Event-driven output capture**: Comprehensive logging of all six PowerShell output streams 5. **Interface-based logging**: Multiple logging implementations for different deployment contexts 6. **Singleton configuration**: Centralized settings management with file fallback logic 7. **Process priority elevation**: Temporary CPU priority boost during execution 8. **Automatic compression**: GZip compression for large payloads to respect IoT Hub limits 9. **Structured error reporting**: Rich error details with inner exception chains 10. **Multiple operational modes**: Debug, Test, Console, Service, and Installer modes This architecture enables the system to execute PowerShell scripts remotely through Azure IoT Hub while maintaining comprehensive telemetry, error handling, and resource management suitable for production IoT deployments. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/IoT/IoTHubService.cs:1-614](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:1-684](), [config/appsettings.json:1-10](), [README.md:1-197]()

It covers connection management, direct method handling (specifically the `ExecuteScript` method), telemetry transmission, and device twin synchronization. ## Purpose and Scope This document describes the PowerShell execution subsystem within IoTPowerShellAgent, centered on the `PowerShellExecutor` class. It covers runspace lifecycle management, concurrency throttling with `SemaphoreSlim`, output stream capture, module preloading strategies, and serialization of PowerShell objects to JSON. For IoT Hub integration and how scripts are invoked via direct methods, see [IoT Hub Integration](#2.1). For error handling and structured error reporting, see [Error Handling and Logging](#2.5). Without preloading, auto-loading can fail with cryptic PSSnapIn errors. Direct path loading bypasses the auto-import mechanism and ensures modules are available before user scripts run. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:314-397]() --- ## Serialization Strategy The executor intelligently serializes PowerShell output based on object complexity. If this is the first access, the singleton initializes by calling `LoadSettings()`. The service then creates an `IoTHubService` instance using connection settings from `ServiceSettings`. After connecting to IoT Hub, the service instantiates `EnvironmentMetricsCollector` and calls `CollectAllMetricsAsync()` to gather environment information. These metrics, combined with runtime metrics from `ProcessUtil`, are sent to IoT Hub as device twin reported properties via `IoTHubService.UpdateTwinAsync()`. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/SettingsService.cs:10-127](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Utilities/EnvironmentMetricsCollector.cs:231-258]() --- ## Configuration Persistence The `SaveSettings` method at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/SettingsService.cs:102-126]() implements the same multi-path fallback strategy as `LoadSettings`, attempting to write to the first writable location. If the directory does not exist, it creates the directory structure using `Directory.CreateDirectory()` at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/SettingsService.cs:116](). The method uses `JsonSerializerOptions { WriteIndented = true }` at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/SettingsService.cs:118]() to produce human-readable JSON with proper indentation. ### Configuration Persistence Paths ```mermaid graph TD SaveSettings["SaveSettings()"] Path1["BaseDirectory/../../config/appsettings.json"] Path2["BaseDirectory/appsettings.json"] Path3["BaseDirectory/config/appsettings.json"] DirCheck1{"Directory.Exists?"} DirCheck2{"Directory.Exists?"} CreateDir["Directory.CreateDirectory()"] Serialize["JsonSerializer.Serialize

If no configuration file existed during initial loading, `SaveSettings` creates the default configuration file, enabling manual editing by administrators. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/SettingsService.cs:102-126]() --- ## Configuration Best Practices ### Default Value Strategy The `ServiceSettings` class provides sensible defaults for all properties: - **`ScriptTimeoutSeconds: 300`** - 5-minute timeout prevents runaway scripts - **`MaxConcurrentRunspaces: 2`** - Conservative limit prevents out-of-memory conditions on resource-constrained devices - **`AutoUpdateIntervalHours: 48`** - Balances update freshness with network overhead - **`TransportType: "Amqp"`** - AMQP provides the best performance and reliability for IoT Hub ### Security Considerations **Connection String Protection**: The `IoTHubConnectionString` contains sensitive credentials. The configuration file should be secured with appropriate NTFS permissions when deployed as a Windows Service running under `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM`. **Alternative Authentication**: The `AzureIotHubHost` and `SharedAccessKey` properties at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/SettingsService.cs:192-198]() provide an alternative to embedding the full connection string, allowing for key rotation without modifying the hostname. ### Environment Metrics Timing The `EnvironmentMetricsCollector` should be invoked during service initialization and periodically during runtime to detect environment changes (e.g., domain join operations, Entra Connect installation). The `CollectAllMetricsAsync` method uses `Task.WhenAll` at [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Utilities/EnvironmentMetricsCollector.cs:242]() to execute WMI queries in parallel, minimizing collection latency. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/SettingsService.cs:132-199](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Utilities/EnvironmentMetricsCollector.cs:231-258]()

# Error Handling and Logging
Relevant source files The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page: - [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/PowerShellErrorDetails.cs](src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/PowerShellErrorDetails.cs) - [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/PowerShellExecutionResult.cs](src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/PowerShellExecutionResult.cs) - [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs](src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs)
This document describes the error handling and logging architecture in IoTPowerShellAgent. It covers how errors are captured from PowerShell execution and other system operations, structured into machine-readable formats, logged to multiple destinations (Windows Event Log, IoT Hub Telemetry), and reported through device twin updates. The logging infrastructure uses a callback-based design to decouple error generation from error reporting, enabling flexible logging strategies for different operational modes. For information about PowerShell script execution mechanics, see [PowerShell Execution Engine](#2.2). For IoT Hub communication patterns, see [IoT Hub Integration](#2.1). For testing error scenarios, see [Unit and Integration Tests](#5.1). --- ## Error Handling Strategy IoTPowerShellAgent implements a multi-layered error handling strategy designed to comprehensively capture, structure, and report errors from distributed IoT devices. Errors are captured at their source, normalized into structured data models, and forwarded through an abstraction layer to multiple destinations. The error handling system addresses four primary failure scenarios: 1. **PowerShell Script Execution Errors**: Syntax errors, runtime exceptions, cmdlet failures, and terminating/non-terminating errors captured from ErrorRecord objects 2. **IoT Hub Communication Failures**: Network timeouts, authentication failures, message size violations, and device twin update errors 3. **Windows API Operation Failures**: P/Invoke call failures, insufficient privileges, and resource access errors 4. **Service Lifecycle Errors**: Service start/stop failures, configuration validation errors, and dependency initialization failures ### Error Flow Architecture ```mermaid graph TB subgraph ErrorSources["Error Generation Sources"] PSExec["PowerShellExecutor

It aggregates multiple error details and provides JSON serialization. **Class Structure:** | Property | Type | Description | |----------|------|-------------| | `Success` | `bool` | Execution success flag | | `Output` | `string` | Serialized output or empty string | | `ErrorMessage` | `string` | Human-readable error summary | | `ErrorDetails` | `List?` | Structured error collection | | `Exception` | `Exception?` | Original exception object | | `RawOutput` | `object?` | Unprocessed PowerShell output | The `ToJson()` method serializes the result using `JsonObject.ConvertToJson()` with support for compression and depth control. Exception objects are automatically converted to `PowerShellErrorDetails` during serialization. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/PowerShellExecutionResult.cs:10-48](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/PowerShellExecutionResult.cs:52-85]() ### PowerShell Stream Error Capture PowerShell exposes six output streams that are captured via event handlers registered in the `BindEvents()` method: | Stream | Handler Method | LogOutputType | Purpose | |--------|---------------|---------------|---------| | Debug | `Debug_DataAdded()` | `Debug` | Debug messages from `Write-Debug` | | Error | `Error_DataAdded()` | `Error` | Non-terminating errors | | Progress | `Progress_DataAdded()` | `Progress` | Progress bars and status updates | | Verbose | `Verbose_DataAdded()` | `Verbose` | Verbose messages from `Write-Verbose` | | Warning | `Warning_DataAdded()` | `Warning` | Warning messages from `Write-Warning` | | Information | `Information_DataAdded()` | `Information` | Information stream (PS 5.0+) | Each handler processes incrementally added data using tracked line counters (`_debugLinesProcessed`, `_errorLinesProcessed`, etc.) to avoid reprocessing previously captured output. #### Stream Event Binding Architecture ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant PSExec as PowerShellExecutor participant PS as PowerShell instance participant Streams as PowerShell.Streams participant Host as DefaultHost PSExec->>PS: Create PowerShell instance PSExec->>PSExec: BindEvents(ps, host) PSExec->>Streams: ps.Streams.Debug.DataAdded += Debug_DataAdded PSExec->>Streams: ps.Streams.Error.DataAdded += Error_DataAdded PSExec->>Streams: ps.Streams.Progress.DataAdded += Progress_DataAdded PSExec->>Streams: ps.Streams.Verbose.DataAdded += Verbose_DataAdded PSExec->>Streams: ps.Streams.Warning.DataAdded += Warning_DataAdded Note over PSExec,Streams: Information stream binding
(PS 5.0+, reflection-based) PSExec->>PS: GetType().GetProperty("Information") PS-->>PSExec: PropertyInfo or null alt Information stream exists PSExec->>Streams: GetEvent("DataAdded") PSExec->>PSExec: CreateDelegate(Information_DataAdded) PSExec->>Streams: AddEventHandler(handler) else Fallback PSExec->>Host: host.OnInformation += Host_OnInformation end Note over PSExec: Script execution begins PS->>Streams: Write-Error "Error message" Streams->>PSExec: Error_DataAdded event PSExec->>PSExec: SendLog(message, LogOutputType.Error) PSExec->>ILogCallback: OnLog(message, Error) ``` **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:210-249](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:79-183]() ### Error Collection and Aggregation When PowerShell execution completes, all errors in `powerShell.Streams.Error` are collected and structured: ``` // From ExecutePowerShellInternal() if (powerShell.Streams.Error.Count > 0) { var errorDetailsList = new List(); StringBuilder errorBuilder = new StringBuilder(); foreach (ErrorRecord error in powerShell.Streams.Error) { // Create structured error details var errorDetails = PowerShellErrorDetails.FromErrorRecord(error); errorDetailsList.Add(errorDetails); // Build human-readable summary string errorMsg = error.Exception?.Message ?? error.ToString(); errorBuilder.AppendLine(errorMsg); // Include inner exceptions in summary var innerException = error.Exception?.InnerException; int innerDepth = 0; while (innerException != null && innerDepth < 5) { errorBuilder.AppendLine($" Inner Exception: {innerException.Message}"); innerException = innerException.InnerException; innerDepth++; } } result.ErrorMessage = errorBuilder.ToString(); result.ErrorDetails = errorDetailsList; result.Success = false; } ``` This produces both a human-readable error message and a structured collection of error details suitable for programmatic analysis and JSON transmission. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:426-466]() --- ## Logging Infrastructure ### ILogCallback Interface The `ILogCallback` interface provides abstraction for logging implementations, allowing different logging strategies based on operational mode without coupling error generation to error reporting. ``` public interface ILogCallback { void OnLog(string message, LogOutputType logType); } ``` **Implementations:** | Implementation | Purpose | Typical Usage | |----------------|---------|---------------| | `EventLogCallback` | Writes to Windows Event Log and forwards to IoT Hub telemetry | Production Windows Service mode | | `CapturingLogCallback` | Captures logs in-memory for test validation | Unit tests and integration tests | | `TestLogCallback` | Outputs to console for debugging | Debug mode and local testing | **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:679-683]() ### LogOutputType Enumeration The `LogOutputType` enum categorizes log messages for filtering, routing, and severity classification: ``` public enum LogOutputType { Information, // General informational messages Debug, // Debug-level diagnostics Verbose, // Verbose operational details Warning, // Warning conditions Error, // Error conditions Progress // Progress indicators } ``` Each type maps to corresponding PowerShell stream types and is used for telemetry message classification when forwarding to IoT Hub. ### SendLog Method and Activity Throttling The `SendLog()` method enforces activity log throttling to prevent log flooding: ``` public void SendLog(string logOutput, LogOutputType logtype) { if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(logOutput)) return; if (_activityLogCounter > _activityLogThreshold) { throw new Exception("Activity Log threshold exceeded."); } ++_activityLogCounter; _logCallback?.OnLog(logOutput, logtype); } ``` The `_activityLogThreshold` is configured via `SettingsService.Instance.Settings.ActivityLogThreshold` and resets for each script execution. This prevents scripts with excessive logging from overwhelming the system or IoT Hub message quotas. **Default Threshold:** Configured in `appsettings.json` (see [Configuration Management](#2.4)) **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:65-77](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:35-44]() --- ## Error Propagation and Exception Handling ### Try-Catch-Finally Pattern PowerShell execution uses comprehensive try-catch-finally blocks to ensure resource cleanup even during error conditions: ```mermaid graph TD Start["ExecutePowerShellInternal()"] --> TryBlock["try block

This ensures proper cancellation semantics when script execution times out (configured via `ScriptTimeoutSeconds` setting). **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:564-570]() ### Semaphore-Based Concurrency Control The `_executionSemaphore` (type: `SemaphoreSlim`) throttles concurrent script executions to prevent resource exhaustion: ``` // Wait for semaphore slot (throttles concurrent executions) await _executionSemaphore!.WaitAsync(cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false); try { // Execute the synchronous PowerShell invocation in a background task return await Task.Run(() => ExecutePowerShellInternal(script, isInlinePowershell, cancellationToken), cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false); } finally { // Always release semaphore slot _executionSemaphore.Release(); } ``` The semaphore is initialized with `MaxConcurrentRunspaces` (default: 2) and uses double-checked locking for thread-safe initialization. The `finally` block guarantees release even if execution throws an exception. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:263-277](), [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:49-63]() --- ## Error Reporting to IoT Hub ### Telemetry Message Format When `EventLogCallback` is used (production mode), log messages are forwarded to IoT Hub as telemetry messages with this structure: ```json { "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:45.123Z", "logType": "Error", "message": "PowerShell script execution failed: The term 'Get-NonexistentCommand' is not recognized...", "deviceId": "device-001" } ``` ### Device Twin Error Reporting Critical errors that prevent service operation are reported via device twin reported properties: ```json { "properties": { "reported": { "serviceStatus": "Error", "lastError": "Failed to connect to IoT Hub: Authentication failed", "lastErrorTime": "2024-01-15T10:30:45.123Z" } } } ``` This allows centralized monitoring dashboards to detect devices in error states without querying individual device logs. ### Error Response in Direct Method Handlers When script execution fails, the `ExecuteScript` direct method returns an error response with structured details: ```json { "status": 400, "payload": { "success": false, "output": "", "errorMessage": "CommandNotFoundException: The term 'Get-NonexistentCommand' is not recognized...", "errorDetails": [ { "message": "The term 'Get-NonexistentCommand' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet...", "exceptionType": "System.Management.Automation.CommandNotFoundException", "category": "ObjectNotFound", "fullyQualifiedErrorId": "CommandNotFoundException", "scriptStackTrace": "at , : line 1" } ], "executionTimeMs": 150 } } ``` HTTP status codes follow this mapping: | Status Code | Condition | |-------------|-----------| | 200 | Script executed successfully | | 400 | Invalid request (missing script, validation failure) | | 408 | Script execution timeout | | 500 | Internal error (exception during execution) | **Sources:** Referenced from architecture diagrams and IoTHubService implementation (see [IoT Hub Integration](#2.1)) --- ## Logging Callback Implementations ### EventLogCallback The `EventLogCallback` implementation writes log messages to Windows Event Log under the "IoTPowerShellAgent" source and forwards them to IoT Hub telemetry. This dual-destination approach ensures logs are available locally (for Windows administrators) and centrally (for cloud monitoring). **Typical Usage:** ``` var logCallback = new EventLogCallback(iotHubService); var executor = new PowerShellExecutor(logCallback); ``` ### CapturingLogCallback The `CapturingLogCallback` captures all log messages in an in-memory collection for test validation. It implements `ILogCallback` and exposes captured logs through a read-only collection. **Typical Usage:** ``` var capturingCallback = new CapturingLogCallback(); var executor = new PowerShellExecutor(capturingCallback); var result = executor.ExecutePowerShell(script, true); // Validate logs were captured Assert.Contains(capturingCallback.Logs, log => log.Type == LogOutputType.Error); ``` This is used extensively in Pester tests (see [Unit and Integration Tests](#5.1)) to validate error handling behavior. ### TestLogCallback The `TestLogCallback` writes log messages directly to `Console.WriteLine()` for debugging during local development. It is used by `LocalIoTTester` in debug and test modes (see [Debug and Test Modes](#3.1)). **Typical Usage:** ``` var testCallback = new TestLogCallback(); var executor = new PowerShellExecutor(testCallback); // All logs appear in console output during execution ``` --- ## Error Handling Best Practices ### Resource Cleanup Guarantees All disposable resources (runspaces, PowerShell instances, output streams) are cleaned up in `finally` blocks to prevent resource leaks even during error conditions: ``` finally { if (runspace != null) { runspace.Close(); runspace.Dispose(); } if (powerShell != null) { powerShell.Dispose(); } if (psobject2 is IDisposable disposable) { disposable.Dispose(); } } ``` **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/PowerShell/PowerShellExecutor.cs:585-600]() ### Defensive Null Checking All error handling code uses defensive null checks to prevent cascading failures during error processing: ``` string errorMsg = error.Exception?.Message ?? error.ToString(); ``` This pattern ensures that even if error objects are malformed, error reporting continues gracefully. ### Structured Error Details for Debugging The recursive capture of inner exceptions (up to 10 levels) provides complete diagnostic context for troubleshooting complex failure scenarios, particularly important for remote IoT devices where interactive debugging is not possible. **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/PowerShellErrorDetails.cs:126-169]()

## Purpose and Scope This document describes the five operational modes supported by IoTPowerShellAgent and the mode selection logic that routes execution to the appropriate runtime environment. Each mode is designed for specific deployment scenarios ranging from production service hosting to local offline development. For detailed information about offline testing workflows, see [Debug and Test Modes](#3.1). For Windows Service lifecycle management and service-specific configuration, see [Windows Service Hosting](#2.3). For IoT Hub connectivity requirements, see [IoT Hub Integration](#2.1). --- ## Mode Overview IoTPowerShellAgent supports five distinct operational modes, each triggered by specific command-line arguments or runtime conditions: | Mode | Trigger | IoT Hub Required | Primary Use Case | |------|---------|------------------|------------------| | **Service Installer** | `install`, `uninstall`, `start`, `stop`, `status`, `update` | No | Service installation and management | | **Windows Service** | `Environment.UserInteractive == false` | Yes | Production deployment | | **Console** | `dotnet run` (no args, UserInteractive=true) | Yes | Development with IoT Hub | | **Debug** | `--debug` or `-d` | No | Interactive local testing | | **Test** | `--test` or `-t` | No | Automated local testing | The mode selection logic is centralized in the `Program.Main` method, which examines command-line arguments and runtime environment to determine the appropriate execution path. **Sources:** [Program.cs:18-57](), [README.md:69-129]() --- ## Mode Selection and Dispatch Logic The following diagram shows how `Program.Main` routes execution to different operational modes based on command-line arguments and the `Environment.UserInteractive` flag: ```mermaid flowchart TD Start["Program.Main(args)"] --> CheckInstaller{"args[0] matches

This mode does not execute PowerShell scripts or connect to IoT Hub. ### Supported Commands The installer recognizes the following commands passed as the first command-line argument: - **`install [orgId]`** - Registers the service with Windows Service Control Manager (SCM) and configures it to run as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` - **`uninstall [orgId]`** - Removes the service registration from SCM - **`start [orgId]`** - Starts the installed service - **`stop [orgId]`** - Stops the running service - **`status [orgId]`** - Displays service status and configuration - **`update [orgId]`** - Updates service configuration The optional `[orgId]` parameter customizes the service name for multi-tenant deployments. ### Detection Logic ```csharp // Program.cs:59-64 private static bool IsInstallerCommand(string command) { string cmd = command.ToLowerInvariant(); return cmd == "install" || cmd == "uninstall" || cmd == "start" || cmd == "stop" || cmd == "status" || cmd == "update"; } ``` ### Execution Flow When an installer command is detected, `Program.Main` delegates to `InstallerProgram.RunInstaller(args)` which performs the requested operation and returns an exit code. No IoT Hub connection or PowerShell execution occurs in this mode. ### Service Account Configuration The installer automatically configures the service to run as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM`, granting full system privileges to executed PowerShell scripts. This configuration is intentional to maximize script execution capabilities but requires strict access control at the IoT Hub level. **Sources:** [Program.cs:20-24](), [Program.cs:59-64](), [README.md:118-131]() --- ## Windows Service Mode (Production) Windows Service mode is the production deployment configuration where the application runs as a background service managed by Windows Service Control Manager. ### Activation Condition This mode activates when `Environment.UserInteractive` returns `false`, indicating the process is running as a Windows Service rather than an interactive console application. ```csharp // Program.cs:40-56 if (Environment.UserInteractive) { // Run as console application for debugging RunAsConsole(args).GetAwaiter().GetResult(); return 0; } else { // Run as Windows Service ServiceBase[] ServicesToRun; ServicesToRun = new ServiceBase[] { new PowerShellExecutorService() }; ServiceBase.Run(ServicesToRun); return 0; } ``` ### Service Lifecycle The `PowerShellExecutorService` class implements the Windows Service lifecycle: 1. **OnStart** - Initializes `IoTHubService`, connects to Azure IoT Hub, starts telemetry reporting 2. **OnStop** - Disconnects from IoT Hub, disposes resources 3. **OnShutdown** - Graceful shutdown handling ### Runtime Characteristics | Characteristic | Value | |----------------|-------| | Process Priority | Elevated to HIGH during script execution, restored to NORMAL afterward | | Service Account | `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` (configured during installation) | | Logging | Windows Event Log + IoT Hub telemetry | | IoT Hub Connection | Required (reads from `appsettings.json`) | | Auto-restart | Configurable via Windows Service Recovery settings | ### Configuration Requirements Windows Service mode requires a valid `IoTHubConnectionString` in `appsettings.json`: ```json { "IoTHubConnectionString": "HostName=your-iothub.azure-devices.net;DeviceId=your-device-id;SharedAccessKey=your-key", "DeviceId": "your-device-id", "ScriptTimeoutSeconds": 300, "MaxConcurrentRunspaces": 2 } ``` **Sources:** [Program.cs:40-56](), [README.md:117-131](), [config/appsettings.json:1-9]() --- ## Console Mode (Development) Console mode provides an interactive development environment with full IoT Hub connectivity. This mode is useful for testing IoT Hub integration scenarios while maintaining visibility into log output. ### Activation Condition Console mode activates when: 1. `Environment.UserInteractive == true` (running in an interactive terminal) 2. No command-line arguments are provided, OR 3. Command-line arguments do not match installer, debug, or test mode triggers Typical activation: `dotnet run` from the project directory. ### Execution Flow Console mode uses reflection to invoke protected lifecycle methods of `PowerShellExecutorService`: ```csharp // Program.cs:204-236 (simplified) private static async Task RunAsConsole(string[] args) { Console.WriteLine("IoTPowerShellAgent - Console Mode"); var service = new PowerShellExecutorService(); // Invoke protected OnStart method var onStartMethod = typeof(PowerShellExecutorService).GetMethod("OnStart", System.Reflection.BindingFlags.NonPublic | System.Reflection.BindingFlags.Instance); onStartMethod?.Invoke(service, new object[] { args }); await Task.Delay(-1); // Wait indefinitely // Invoke protected OnStop method on exit var onStopMethod = typeof(PowerShellExecutorService).GetMethod("OnStop", System.Reflection.BindingFlags.NonPublic | System.Reflection.BindingFlags.Instance); onStopMethod?.Invoke(service, null); } ``` ### Use Cases - **IoT Hub Integration Testing** - Verify direct method handlers, telemetry transmission, device twin updates - **Configuration Validation** - Test connection strings and configuration settings - **Log Inspection** - View real-time log output in console before deploying as a service - **Debugging** - Attach debugger to troubleshoot IoT Hub communication issues ### Differences from Windows Service Mode | Aspect | Console Mode | Windows Service Mode | |--------|-------------|---------------------| | Process Account | Current user | `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` | | Log Output | Console + Event Log + IoT Hub | Event Log + IoT Hub | | Lifecycle | Manual (Ctrl+C to exit) | Managed by SCM | | Auto-restart | No | Yes (configurable) | **Sources:** [Program.cs:40-44](), [Program.cs:204-236](), [README.md:108-115]() --- ## Debug Mode (Interactive Testing) Debug mode provides an interactive REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) for testing PowerShell script execution without requiring IoT Hub connectivity. This mode is ideal for rapid iteration during script development. ### Activation ```bash dotnet run -- --debug # or dotnet run -- -d ``` ### Key Features - **No IoT Hub Required** - Uses `LocalIoTTester` for offline execution - **Interactive Shell** - Accepts PowerShell commands directly - **Base64 Support** - Test base64-encoded scripts with `base64:` prefix - **Environment Metrics** - View system metrics with `metrics` command - **Sample Scripts** - Run pre-configured test with `sample` command ### Interactive Commands ``` PS> Get-Date # Execute PowerShell directly PS> Get-Process | Select-Object -First 5 # Pipeline commands PS> base64:RwBlAHQALQBEAGEAdABlAA== # Base64-encoded script PS> metrics # Show environment metrics PS> sample # Run sample test PS> help # Display help PS> exit # Exit debug mode ``` ### Implementation Debug mode instantiates `LocalIoTTester` and enters a loop that reads user input and executes scripts: ```csharp // Program.cs:66-165 (key sections) private static async Task RunDebugMode() { var tester = new LocalIoTTester(); bool running = true; while (running) { Console.Write("PS> "); string? input = Console.ReadLine(); // Handle special commands (exit, help, metrics, sample) // Handle base64: prefix // Execute via tester.ExecuteScriptLocally() } } ``` For comprehensive documentation of debug mode features and workflows, see [Debug and Test Modes](#3.1). **Sources:** [Program.cs:27-30](), [Program.cs:66-165](), [README.md:69-95]() --- ## Test Mode (Automated Testing) Test mode executes a single PowerShell script or test scenario and exits, making it suitable for automated testing pipelines and CI/CD integration. ### Activation and Options ```bash # Run default sample test dotnet run -- --test # Execute custom script dotnet run -- --test --script="Get-Date" # Test base64-encoded script dotnet run -- --test --script= --base64 # Test environment metrics collection dotnet run -- --test --metrics ``` ### Execution Flow Test mode parses command-line arguments to determine which test to execute: ```csharp // Program.cs:167-202 (simplified) private static async Task RunTestMode(string[] args) { var tester = new LocalIoTTester(); if (args.Length > 1 && args[1] == "--base64") { await tester.TestWithBase64Script(); } else if (args.Length > 1 && args[1].StartsWith("--script=")) { string script = args[1].Substring("--script=".Length); bool isBase64 = args.Length > 2 && args[2] == "--base64"; await tester.ExecuteScriptLocally(script, false, isBase64); } else if (args.Length > 1 && args[1] == "--metrics") { await tester.TestEnvironmentMetrics(); } else { await tester.TestWithSampleScript(); } } ``` ### LocalIoTTester Integration Both Debug and Test modes use `LocalIoTTester` to simulate IoT Hub direct method calls without actual cloud connectivity. `LocalIoTTester` instantiates a `PowerShellExecutor` and returns a `ScriptExecutionResponse` matching the structure used by `IoTHubService.ExecuteScriptMethodHandler`. For detailed information about `LocalIoTTester` capabilities and test helper classes, see [Debug and Test Modes](#3.1). **Sources:** [Program.cs:34-38](), [Program.cs:167-202](), [README.md:98-106](), [LocalIoTTester.cs:15-112]() --- ## Mode Comparison Matrix The following table provides a comprehensive comparison of runtime characteristics across all operational modes: | Characteristic | Service Installer | Windows Service | Console | Debug | Test | |----------------|------------------|----------------|---------|-------|------| | **Requires IoT Hub** | No | Yes | Yes | No | No | | **Executes PowerShell** | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | | **Interactive** | No | No | No | Yes | No | | **Exit Behavior** | Immediate | Runs until stopped | Runs until Ctrl+C | Runs until `exit` | Exits after execution | | **Log Destination** | Console | Event Log + IoT Hub | Console + Event Log + IoT Hub | Console | Console | | **Primary Class** | `InstallerProgram` | `PowerShellExecutorService` | `PowerShellExecutorService` | `LocalIoTTester` | `LocalIoTTester` | | **Configuration Required** | None | `appsettings.json` | `appsettings.json` | None | None | | **Use Case** | Service management | Production | Development | Script testing | Automated testing | **Sources:** [Program.cs:18-57]() --- ## Configuration Requirements by Mode Different operational modes have different configuration dependencies: ```mermaid graph LR subgraph "No Configuration Required" ServiceInstaller["Service Installer Mode"] DebugMode["Debug Mode"] TestMode["Test Mode"] end subgraph "IoT Hub Configuration Required" WindowsService["Windows Service Mode"] ConsoleMode["Console Mode"] end subgraph "appsettings.json" IoTHubConnectionString["IoTHubConnectionString"] DeviceId["DeviceId"] ModuleId["ModuleId (optional)"] ScriptTimeoutSeconds["ScriptTimeoutSeconds"] MaxConcurrentRunspaces["MaxConcurrentRunspaces"] end WindowsService --> IoTHubConnectionString WindowsService --> DeviceId WindowsService --> ModuleId WindowsService --> ScriptTimeoutSeconds WindowsService --> MaxConcurrentRunspaces ConsoleMode --> IoTHubConnectionString ConsoleMode --> DeviceId ConsoleMode --> ModuleId ConsoleMode --> ScriptTimeoutSeconds ConsoleMode --> MaxConcurrentRunspaces ``` ### appsettings.json Location Resolution The application searches for `appsettings.json` in multiple locations with the following priority: 1. Current working directory 2. Executable directory 3. `config/` subdirectory relative to executable 4. If not found, creates a default template file This multi-path resolution ensures the application can locate configuration in both development (`dotnet run`) and deployment scenarios. **Sources:** [config/appsettings.json:1-9]() --- ## Mode Selection Best Practices ### Development Workflow 1. **Initial Development** - Use **Debug Mode** for rapid script iteration without IoT Hub setup 2. **Integration Testing** - Use **Console Mode** to test IoT Hub connectivity and direct method handling 3. **Automated Testing** - Use **Test Mode** in CI/CD pipelines for validation 4. **Production Deployment** - Use **Service Installer Mode** to register, then **Windows Service Mode** for runtime ### Troubleshooting - **Service won't start** - Check Event Viewer for errors; verify `appsettings.json` exists and contains valid IoT Hub connection string - **Debug mode command not recognized** - Ensure using `--` separator: `dotnet run -- --debug` - **PowerShell execution fails** - Test in Debug mode first to isolate script issues from IoT Hub connectivity - **Configuration not found** - Service mode searches multiple paths; use Console mode to verify configuration loading **Sources:** [README.md:183-189]() --- ## Summary IoTPowerShellAgent's five operational modes provide flexibility for different deployment and development scenarios: - **Service Installer Mode** handles Windows Service lifecycle management - **Windows Service Mode** provides production-ready background execution with `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` privileges - **Console Mode** enables development with full IoT Hub integration and visible logging - **Debug Mode** offers interactive testing without cloud dependencies - **Test Mode** supports automated testing and CI/CD integration The mode selection logic in `Program.Main` automatically routes execution based on command-line arguments and runtime environment, ensuring appropriate behavior for each scenario without requiring code changes between development and production deployments. **Sources:** [Program.cs:18-57]()

Maximum payload size: 10MB - If `IsBase64Encoded` is `true`, the script is decoded before execution - Empty or whitespace-only scripts are rejected **Sources:** Documented in system architecture diagrams --- ### ScriptExecutionResponse The `ExecuteScript` direct method returns a JSON response with the following structure: ```json { "Success": true, "Output": "Friday, January 10, 2025 3:45:23 PM", "ErrorMessage": "", "ExecutionTimeMs": 127, "IsCompressed": false, "OriginalSize": 0, "CompressedSize": 0 } ``` | Field | Type | Description | |-------|------|-------------| | `Success` | `bool` | Execution success indicator | | `Output` | `string` | Script output (may be GZip compressed and Base64-encoded if > 1KB) | | `ErrorMessage` | `string` | Error summary if `Success` is `false` | | `ErrorDetails` | `PowerShellErrorDetails[]?` | Structured error information with inner exception chains | | `ExecutionTimeMs` | `long` | Execution duration in milliseconds | | `IsCompressed` | `bool` | Whether `Output` is compressed (compression threshold: 1KB) | | `OriginalSize` | `int` | Original output size in bytes (if compressed) | | `CompressedSize` | `int` | Compressed output size in bytes (if compressed) | **HTTP Status Codes:** - `200`: Successful execution (may contain script errors in `ErrorMessage`) - `400`: Invalid request (e.g., payload too large, missing script) - `408`: Timeout (script exceeded `ScriptTimeoutSeconds`) - Concurrency and Threading Primitives ### SemaphoreSlim Usage The `PowerShellExecutor` uses `SemaphoreSlim` to enforce a concurrency limit on script executions, preventing resource exhaustion on IoT devices. **Implementation Pattern:** ```csharp private readonly SemaphoreSlim _semaphore; public PowerShellExecutor(int maxConcurrent) { _semaphore = new SemaphoreSlim(maxConcurrent, maxConcurrent); } public async Task ExecutePowerShellAsync(...) { await _semaphore.WaitAsync(cancellationToken); try { // Execute script in isolated runspace } finally { _semaphore.Release(); } } ``` **Configuration:** The maximum concurrent executions is controlled by the `MaxConcurrentRunspaces` setting (default: 2). **Sources:** Documented in system architecture diagrams --- ### CancellationToken Handling All asynchronous operations support `CancellationToken` for graceful cancellation: 1. **Timeout Enforcement:** IoTHubService creates a `CancellationTokenSource` with `ScriptTimeoutSeconds` duration 2. **Script Cancellation:** Token is passed through to PowerShell runspace via `PowerShell.BeginInvoke` 3. **Cleanup:** Finally blocks ensure resources are disposed even when cancelled **Pattern:** ```csharp using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(timeoutSeconds)); var result = await _executor.ExecutePowerShellAsync(script, isInline, cts.Token); ``` **Sources:** Documented in system architecture diagrams --- ## JSON Serialization ### JsonObject Utility The `JsonObject` class provides PowerShell-aware JSON serialization that correctly handles PSObject types, complex nested objects, and circular references. **Location:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Utilities/JsonObject.cs]() #### Key Methods **ConvertToJson(object? obj, ConvertToJsonContext context): string?** Serializes an object to JSON with configurable depth, enum handling, and output compression. **ConvertFromJson(string json): object?** Deserializes JSON string to PowerShell-compatible objects. #### ConvertToJsonContext Configuration structure for JSON serialization: | Property | Type | Default | Description | |----------|------|---------|-------------| | `maxDepth` | `int` | `1024` | Maximum object graph depth (prevents stack overflow) | | `enumsAsStrings` | `bool` | `true` | Serialize enums as string names rather than numeric values | | `compressOutput` | `bool` | `false` | Compress whitespace in output JSON | **Usage in PowerShellExecutionResult:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/PowerShellExecutionResult.cs:56-71]() **Sources:** [src/IoTPowerShellAgent/Core/PowerShellExecutionResult.cs:52-84]() --- ## Summary This reference documents the foundational types that comprise the IoTPowerShellAgent's core API: **Interfaces:** - `IIoTHubService` - Azure IoT Hub integration contract - `IPowerShellExecutor` - PowerShell execution contract - `ILogCallback` - Logging abstraction **Data Structures:** - `PowerShellExecutionResult` - Complete execution outcome with output and errors - `PowerShellErrorDetails` - Recursive error representation with inner exception support - `DirectMethodRequest` / `ScriptExecutionResponse` - IoT Hub message schemas **Configuration:** - `SettingsService` - Centralized configuration singleton - `appsettings.json` schema with IoT Hub connection and execution parameters **Utilities:** - `JsonObject` - PowerShell-aware JSON serialization - `SemaphoreSlim` - Concurrency control for script execution - `CancellationToken` - Timeout and cancellation support For detailed implementation documentation, see the subsections: - [IoTHubService API](#4.1) - Complete API reference for Azure IoT Hub integration - [PowerShellExecutor API](#4.2) - PowerShell execution engine details - [Utilities and Helpers](#4.3) - Supporting classes and interop

## Purpose and Scope This document provides a complete API reference for the `IoTHubService` class, which serves as the primary integration point with Azure IoT Hub. The `IoTHubService` manages device/module connections, handles direct method invocations for script execution, sends telemetry, and updates device twin properties. This document covers the `IoTHubService` class API, the `IIoTHubService` interface, and associated data models (`ScriptExecutionRequest`, `ScriptExecutionResponse`).
